utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It's unfortunate that due to circumstances at the Detention Unit we've had to have a late start today. We would propose to try and minimise the effect of that by sitting longer for each of two periods so that hopefully we might manage an hour and 40 or an hour and 45 minutes for each sitting session and just have the one break in the middle. Ms. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: If I may address the Chamber on one evidentiary matter that's peripherally related to the testimony today. On 10th of June, 2009, Mr. -- General Vasiljevic was testifying and we had called up a document Mr. Djurdjic had at D003-2633, and this is reflected in the transcript on that date at 5863, line 12. The document that was loaded in at that number was the incorrect number or the incorrect document, excuse me, it was a 3rd Army combat report dated the 29th of April, 1999. General Vasiljevic looked at the document. He attested to it being the 13th of April, 1999, which is the document it should have been. We all actually looked at the document but nobody caught the error that it was the wrong document on the screen. And it was tendered into evidence as D190. The second document that was called right after it was actually the exact same document, the proper 29th of April document, and then that was admitted as D191. So what we have is a duplicate at D190 and D191. We would like to use the 13th April, 1999, document -- or we'd like to have it in evidence, and we're wondering if it would be possible to substitute that in the e-court system at this time as the proper document. Or if you prefer, we can file something on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you see any difficulty, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think leave will be granted to substitute the correct document as the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I leave it to you to work it out with the Court Officer how to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. O'LEARY
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now if we could have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Once again, if I could remind you the affirmation you made still applies. We apologise it was -- there has been a delayed start today because of a fire which has delayed arrangements, so you were kept waiting unexpectedly. Now Mr. Djurdjic will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we were very fast so that there are some imprecise things left in the transcript, so before the end of the day today or before we begin today I would like to correct that and I ask you kindly to continue slowly with your answers in a professorial manner, and I'm also going to do my best to put my questions slowly. General, yesterday on page 7892, line 18, it was said "General Lukovic." Line 17, 21, it also says "General Lukovic." Am I correct if I say that actually it was General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to see that. I don't know what exactly this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's line -- actually page 7892, line 18. It's about the reports by the Joint Command and reporting before the 21st of July. General Bakovic told me that this was on the basis of his agreement with General Lukovic that they should send us certain information so that we could use that when we make our assessments.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about General Lukic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have page 7962, lines 12 to 18. The General Staff tried to do that. There was an order of the 18th of April. I believe that it was received on the 18th of April and the decision was not implemented because the explanation that was given was that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior did not receive the identical order from the Ministry of the Interior as the top ministry -- as the top officer in the ministry. Should it actually state that the organs of the minister did not receive the identical order from the minister of internal affairs as the highest official at the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to correct the transcript here, but we can do it like this. According to your knowledge at the time, Mr. Minic, what was his state position at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I know, he was the president of the council of citizens in the Federal Assembly. I believe that that was his post, and I believe that he was at the same time the director of the railways. I heard that in an informal conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me the post held by Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the vice-president in the -- of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually federal -- the prime minister of the federal government in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andjelkovic, can you tell me what was his post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was the minister for sports and youth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this in the Republic of Serbia, the government in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, in the Government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Matkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Matkovic was responsible for the economy. I don't know if at the time he was a minister, but he was also the director of the steel works in Smederevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned Mr. Andro Milosavljevic. Do you know what his position was, where he worked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he worked at the ministry, one of the ministries, and he was in charge of resolving the outstanding matters in Kosovo and Metohija, in terms of regular supplies and care for the Serbs and Albanians in Kosovo. I really didn't have any contacts with him. It's something that I heard more from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct if I were to say that this function was in the republican government of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had this post in the republican government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On page 8002, lines 1 and 2, in response to a question in 1998 was there resubordination between the army and the military. My question was between the army and the police, actually. So this is something that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That would be that. I would now ask for 65 ter Exhibit 01430.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to look at the signature and the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It seems that you are the author of this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we can look at the first page. I'm interested in the first paragraph regarding these assertions that the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and especially in Metohija recently is becoming even more complex due to the Siptar terrorist pressure at the civilian population in order to prevent their return to inhabited areas. Could we please --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a little more about these statements that you made here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period in early September, terrorist activities continued against members of the army. And the terrorist forces continued to try, by exerting pressure on the civilian population, to -- particularly those of the Catholic faith in the area of Baranski Lug, which includes the area of 20 to 30 villages - by burning haystacks and killing their cattle, burning their houses, and forcing them to take up weapons and to fight against members of the army and the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, the police -- actually, that is one of the most characteristic cases. There were some others in the areas around the outposts in the area of the 53rd Border Battalion. This is the area of Has towards Albania -- actually, it's to the west of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, this occurrence of the abuse of civilians and not permitting them to return to their homes even though the operations were over was something that General Djordjevic pointed to at a meeting on the 14th [as interpreted] of September when you remarked that the civilians should be returned to their villages by force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did include those occurrences in places where this was a characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like a correction in the transcript. I didn't say the 14th of September. I said the 4th of September, that it was a meeting on the 4th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may have meant the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it's possible. I'm not sure, actually, what I said. Thank you, Your Honour. Could we tender this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00337.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like 65 ter document 01433, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document of the 15th of September, and would you believe me when I look at the last page I can see that MDj/MV drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I worked on these documents that refer to the areas of responsibilities of units on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember how these areas of responsibility pursuant to this order were established?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the principle and the order I received from General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document for adoption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00338.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, General, according to what you know, who was in charge of the police units in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say with a great degree of certainty for 1998 that this was the MUP staff in Pristina. I personally did not see any order or document indicating who would be in charge, but in view of what I heard from General Pavkovic he stressed that General Lukic was the commander of the MUP staff in Pristina. In 1999 I went to a different duty and I no longer had contacts with people from the Ministry of the Interior or any civilians who attended the meetings of the Joint Command, except for Mr. Andjelkovic on three occasions. And I already referred to those occasions before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if you know if in 1998 -- in 1998 which police units took part in these anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am well aware of this because I received a review from the MUP staff of the units that were being brought to the area of Kosovo and Metohija, and those are the following units: Ten detachments of 400 to 600 men in strength, so they're of different compositions and different strengths. I know that those detachments were initially deployed as follows: Two detachments from the Uzice area, I don't know from which municipalities, but I know that they referred to them as the Uzice Detachments. They were deployed in the Kosovska Mitrovica and Srbica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really think of the deployment, but can you please tell me which unit these ten detachments were from. What police units this was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the PJPs, Posebne Jedinice Policije.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me which other police units were in Kosovo, their names, not where they were deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the SAJ, the unit for special operations of the state security, and also companies of MUP from the secretariats -- seven secretariats in the Kosovo and Metohija area, and there were a total of ten companies all together, two secretariats had contributed two companies each as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the companies that you mentioned at the end as being from Kosovo, these were Posebne Jedinice Policije, Special Police units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were part of the seven secretariats that covered the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The principle of forming all the PJP units in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia was the same, where several secretariats would contribute detachments so that one detachment was made up of troops from several secretariats?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. One secretariat was not able to form these units, but five or six secretariats would form one detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if you know which department the Jedinica za Specijalne Operacije belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they belonged to the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the commander of the -- unit for special operations commander was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Legija was the commander, namely Milorad Lukovic, a.k.a. Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know -- or rather, what do you know about the reinforcements of the staff when the anti-terrorist actions in Kosovo and Metohija began, the joint military and police actions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what -- how large the staff was and how it was established. What I do know is that after a meeting in Belgrade held on the 21st of July, 1998, at a meeting which was in the evening hours, I saw Mr. Djordjevic and Mr. Obrad Stevanovic. I apologise. I'm not sure whether I actually saw Obrad that very evening, but Mr. Djordjevic, yes, for certain. But whether Obrad came along with him or not I'm not sure of that. I did see him a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, did you know at the time that General Djordjevic and General Obrad Stevanovic were assistant ministers for the interior, assistants to Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After October 1998 did you have occasion to see General Djordjevic at -- in Kosovo and Metohija ever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I had no occasion to see him because General Pavkovic assigned me to other assignments that had to do with the arrival of the OSCE Mission and the deployment of our units in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us that you saw General Djordjevic on the 19th of April, 1999. Aside from that day, did you ever see him in Kosovo and Metohija in the course of 1999 up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already said that we received an order on the 18th from Belgrade. It's possible that I am mistaken, but maybe by a day only, but that was the only time that I saw General Djordjevic and Obrad Stevanovic in Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of 1998, other than in the meetings that you mentioned where you took notes, outside of these meetings did you have any contacts with General Djordjevic or any type of communication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had very infrequent contacts with him, but there was an occasion when I was supposed to exchange information and coordinate my work with MUP staff. And since I didn't find the person that I was looking for, namely Colonel Adamovic, I went to see the duty officers at the duty service. And I found General Djordjevic there. We exchanged greetings. And I noticed that there were some three or four police officers who were monitoring some activities of the Siptar terrorist forces on the screens in front of them. I think they had some tapes, videotapes, and this was following the events in Ovcarevo village and the general just briefly commented. He said, These were the documents that we seized in Ovcarevo village. There is a lot of -- there are a lot of documents there. And this was actually confirmed later on in a meeting where Mr. Sainovic, I think, said that it would be a good idea if the state security organs and military security organs reviewed and studied these documents in order to find out what the deployment of the Kosovo terrorist units in Kosovo was and to use that material in the best possible way. I saw this, and for some five minutes or so perhaps I myself could view this on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, the notes or the minutes that you took in these meetings, tell us, please, these notes were not minutes proper, but rather they were notes that were to serve you and help you in your work. Am I correct if I say then that that is the reason why you did not re-type these notes and produce documents that would be then filed in the protocol of the operations department of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the main reason. I mean, General Pavkovic never asked or ordered me to prepare any document following this meeting. I took the notes for my own purposes - and I stressed this earlier - and I only jotted down those details and facts that I felt might be of use to my command in their assessment of the Siptar terrorist forces' strength. And in fact this notebook was -- I kept it with me all the time until I handed it over to the -- to my subordinate officer who then actually chaired the last five meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P1229.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you've already seen this document. Mr. Hannis presented it to you. It is a document of September 22nd [as interpreted], 1998. He referred you to the heading which says -- which reads: "Implementation of the fifth stage of the plan for combatting terrorism." Now, if I look at the second page I see that it says -- the initials there are BV. You were not the author of this document, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is an NP initial, that's General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's NP, and there is also his signature there. Now what I would like to know is what was the fourth stage if this one is the fifth stage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth stage implied the routing of Siptar terrorist forces in some areas where they re-emerged; in other words, this was just the second and third stage, in fact, once again renewed because unexpectedly some of these terrorist forces actually re-appeared in some areas in Kosovo where we had not foreseen that it was possible at all for them to reach there, for instance, the Jezero mountains. And according to our assessment, it was not expected that there would be an amassing of terrorist forces there. The -- then there was an emergence of the terrorist forces in Podujevo, next west of Pristina, and even in Gnjilane and Kosovska Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have Exhibit D004-3000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document from the forward command post of the 3rd Army signed by General Dusan Samardzic, the commander, whereby he approves the establishment of eight new combat groups. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this document the 26th of September or the 22nd? The transcript records the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's dated the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that in the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00339.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have exhibit -- or rather, document 65 ter 04036.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, were you aware of the contents of the analysis produced by the command of the 3rd Army dated October 2nd, 1998, which document we see in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, and for the most part I was aware of it while it was being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, am I correct in saying that there is -- there are no indications whatsoever in this document that the Pristina Corps actually failed to implement the decisions from the army command for the period to which this report relates?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. From this analysis I can see no objections or no remarks to the effect that the command of the Pristina Corps was not abiding 100 per cent by the commands of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 5 in English and 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we have already seen the description of the stages and what they entailed. I think this document reflects that clearly, how everything transpired, but look at this second paragraph on page 4 here. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the relevant document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you quoting, Mr. Djurdjic? Is it 4.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's actually 3 and then we see it says "negative experiences," and then we have -- I apologise, actually this is at the bottom of page 4 in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the bottom of page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, can you see this last paragraph, that's in the last paragraph, requests were made by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So, General -- and we are on page 4 of the B/C/S as well. That's okay. So, General, this paragraph here "requests were made by the army," am I correct that the support was provided in depth to MUP units and that it was not used for any other tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was in the third stage where the army provides support to MUP in lifting the blockade of the main roads. And we both knew and were certain that MUP alone was not capable nor did it have sufficient forces to lift the blockade of these three main communication routes. And I can say with certainty that the army used a lot of -- applied a lot of effort and together with MUP they finally managed, after fierce fighting, to break-up or destroy the bunkers - especially on the communication lines Klina-Pristina-Pec - bunkers made of reinforced concrete. And we could not believe that it was possible for terrorists, by just using civilians, to build up all these shelters and protective structures. And I myself was able to see this in Iglarevo, where a portion of our units provided support to a MUP unit from the 15th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 7 of the English version and page 6 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this paragraph, 4.3, proposed measures, and then see under the third paragraph where it says "by using larger forces, larger MUP forces ..."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, is this also another bit of evidence that shows that the Joint Command actually had no command responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... an ultimate issue in this case on a legal conclusion that he's not entitled to opine on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis has a valid point, Mr. Djurdjic. You may be able to get something from the witness by asking other questions, but you can't come in in this way asking this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, here under the proposed measures, this paragraph, does the command of the 3rd Army propose that in future whenever units of the MUP are engaged together with the army, that there should be an organ to coordinate the activities with MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that in the earlier period there was no such body created for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that does not mean that because that function was actually performed by the operations and training organ of the Pristina Corps and some elements of the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are now talking about coordination, but what I am referring to is a body or an organ that will actually direct such future joint operations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, up until then there was no such body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a proposal of measures for the future.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coordination is a process which does not entail just the preparation of documents. It is also a process that is active, both in the course of and following a completed combat operation, so that now there is a proposal that during and after combat operations there should be a body to coordinate the work of the military and the MUP so that they shouldn't fire at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that should be done by a new body that was to be established; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a document we see of October 2nd, 1998, so this means that there was no such body in existence at this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you're moving from the idea of there being a person or a group of people at a forward command control post to coordinate on the ground, in the operational spot coordination, to the proposition which you just put at the very end that there was no such body in existence to coordinate. The witness has been at pains to try to point out to you that coordination involves a lot of things, one of them is when there are two operational forces in the one area. I think as he himself put it, it's important to ensure that two friendly forces aren't firing at each other. That's one form of coordination. And this reference seems to be dealing with that. There may be much higher levels of coordination in other parts of the controlling command. Now, you seem to be assuming that there can only be one point of coordination in your questions, and I think the witness was trying to point out to you that some other situation than that obtained. Now, you may want to explore this more with the witness if you've grasped what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you clarify for us, please, the question of the organ that should coordinate a number of the units of the MUP and the army pursuant to the measures contained in this order of the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we understood this in the way that the army commander was insisting that the coordination within the MUP staff and the army be improved from planning with the emphasis on the implementation of combat assignments at all levels. I don't know that there was a special organ allocated to carry out coordination. At the staff and the corps level that was this exchange in the plan part at the level of combat groups, and at the level of MUP detachments the coordination was carried out by the commander of the brigade and the combat group and on the other side the detachment commander -- or rather, the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Well, the proposal here is to appoint an organ in future who would -- that would be in charge of all of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00340.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Exhibit D004-3036.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we're now going to look at one combat report of the 15th of September, 1998, from the 3rd Army command -- the 15th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at page 2 of the English version and page 2 of the B/C/S version. And can we look at item marked with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the 15th of October, 1998. The situation in the territory, in that paragraph it is stated in the first paragraph that: "... 3.000 armed non-uniformed terrorists in the area of Donje Ljupce-Majance-Kisela Banja-Gornje Ljupce-Popovo, Podujevo municipality ..." Could you please tell us a little bit more about this and how this happened that such a number of terrorists appeared in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do -- I am aware of this piece of information, and I know that this is an area that is called the Teneslovski Teznac [phoen] and it spreads from Pristina towards Podujevo. Teneslovski Teznac. And in that area -- or actually, before smaller groups of terrorists were noted there. And then in this period, in mid-October, large numbers of terrorists assembled and there were intense attacks on the MUP and army units on the roads leading to central Serbia. There were an exceptional number of attacks from the Bajgora slopes. This is an area between Kosovska Mitrovica and Podujevo. It is impassable, sparsely populated, and for the most part the terrorists from the Podujevo municipality and some from the Vucitrn municipality participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00341.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D004-3030.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in this document of the 17th of October, 1998, again Podujevo is mentioned that the KLA had returned to the lines they had before they were scattered. They're talking about the villages of Ljubince, Kisela Banja, Popovo, and other villages. This previous answer of yours would refer to these territories as well and what happened on the 17th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same kind of general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But what did the KLA take advantage of in order to return to this territory from which they had been driven away? Was it due to the withdrawal of our forces or ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our forces did -- were not so numerous, neither were the MUP units in such numbers to be able to control and hold the entire territory. Mostly in that narrow area we held five or six key points for purposes of regular logistics supplies of the units from Serbia or units that received their supplies from the Malo Kosovo area or from the Podujevo municipality. The terrorists, being aware that we didn't have enough manpower to cover the whole area - and I already said that this was an area that was full of forests, it was not easily passable, and even the combat equipment tanks could not be used in certain areas -- actually, we're talking about the southern slopes of Mount Kopaonik which in that area is quite impassable and you are not able to use heavy equipment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that later you had some assignments that had to do with the Kosovo Verification Mission. Were members of the KLA using the international situation in order to occupy territories that they had been pushed back from, that they were returning to now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a period when -- I think on the 16th the agreement was signed, and I think it was Mr. Sainovic specifically who was involved in that. At that time, we were carrying out certain movements of troops pursuant to the agreement with the OSCE. Now we're talking about the 15th and the 20th of October, that period. Up until the end of the year we pulled our units back, and from what I know the MUP pulled their forces back to the barracks except for the border units; seven combat groups in the border area, that was something that was in keeping with the strict OSCE agreement; and three tactical groups, three mixed companies that had been deployed at three key points in the area of Volujak mountain near Glina, Iglarevo, which is on the Pristina-Glina road; and one mixed group on the Dulje pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're talking about the Kosovo Verification Mission, we mentioned them, do you have any information about the misuse of the mandate by members of the Kosovo Verification Mission during their stay in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and in the territory of Yugoslavia generally from, let's say, late October until the 20th of March, 1998 -- actually, until March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some contacts with some representatives of the OSCE. Once there were some allegations that our reconnaissance organs fired at their vehicles; and General Pavkovic sent me, he personally sent me, to investigate this matter, to meet with those representatives, and to establish if there had really been any firing at them or not. Not to go into any more detail I'm going to explain briefly that previously I checked what the scouts, the soldiers, had told me and I established reliably that there had been no firing but that due to the driving downhill of a combat vehicle there was gas let out from the tires or the exhaust which sounded like fire from a machine-gun. When I showed the representatives this, he was convinced that there had been no fire that was opened, and he accepted that the army did not fire at their vehicle. I cannot really say anything in particular about misuse or abuse of their position, but it is a fact that OSCE representatives tolerated the provocations on the part of Siptar terrorist forces, attacks on check-points, attacks on mixed units and companies that we had to intervene several times, both General Pavkovic and other organs of the command. But I have to say they accepted that but there didn't seem to be any effort made in order to prevent these activities by the Siptar forces, nothing was achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Defence Exhibit 289, please -- Exhibit D179.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, were you aware that this directive was adopted? We can see that it's called Grom 3, Thunder 3, and this was in January 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that this directive refers to the use of the military in the event of the arrival of the multi-national NATO brigade in the KiM area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It refers only to the strategic formations - does it not? - this directive, the 1st, 2nd, and the 3rd Army, the RVPO [as interpreted] Department, and the KSJ command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 04305 document on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we do that, was there a document of the 17th of October that you intended to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I would like to tender document D00433 -- 43030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just check that we're getting back to the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can assist, the first one was on the 15th of October, 1998, and this one D004-3030 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and then I think this document you referred to but you did not tender, combat report of the 17th of October? You would like it to be received? It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00342.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now you were seeking a further document when I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your help, Your Honour. I asked for document on the 65 ter list 04305, if we can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, we are seeing now on our screen an order of the 3rd Army command of the 27th of January, 1999. Can you please explain to us a little bit about this order. We see that this refers to Grom 3 and what connection is it then with the directive and how does it relate to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Chief of the General Staff on the 16th of January issued the directive Thunder 3, and then on the basis of that directive the command of the 3rd Army approached the drafting of the order for the use of the 3rd Army -- that relates to the same tasks issued in the directive by the Chief of the General Staff in Thunder 3, which is the prevention of the forceful entry of the NATO brigade and the breaking up of the Siptar terrorist forces. And that corresponds to the order of the commander of the 3rd Army that was passed down to the command of the Pristina Corps, where the Pristina Corps command drafted its own order containing the same tasks included at the level of the General Staff and at the level of the command of the 3rd Army but on the territory of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tendering this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00343.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you now clarify certain things. As the result of this operation Thunder 3, am I correct that an order was issued to rout and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in Mala and Velika Drenica, Podujevo and this was to be done by the Pristina Corps? And we can also see Exhibit P889 if that may be of assistance. General, is this one of the documents that was produced in the aftermath of Grom 3 of that -- this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment that the directive was issued by the Chief of the General Staff, the commander of the 3rd arm [as interpreted], and they -- pursuant to the order of the commander of the Pristina Corps, which deal with activities to break-up Siptar terrorist forces, there have been no separate decisions issued, but rather pursuant to the already mentioned directives and orders these were implemented and made operational in the preparations in order to prevent the arrival of the multi-national NATO brigade while at the same time breaking up and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the areas of their arrival. In other words, in the area of Malo Kosovo, Drenica, and Malisevo, these areas were on the outskirt of the assault and landing area of the NATO forces; and the commander of the army, bearing this in mind, developed a plan in order to break up and destroy Siptar terrorist forces on the edges of -- along the edges of these assault areas. And I was ordered by General Pavkovic to provide support to the command of the Pristina Corps in preparing these documents together with the air force officers from the General Staff of the army, who were assigned to the Kosovo Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more clarification, please. In March -- in other words, as of March 22, 1999, up until, I believe, April 16th we have seen a number of orders entitled -- rather, bearing the heading of the Joint Command and that deal with the decisions relating to Malisevo, Drenica, Malo Kosovo, and Zegra. How did -- or did these decisions tie-in with this directive of the 3rd Army and the order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army and the command -- the order of the 3rd Army and the order of the Pristina Corps provided the basis for routing terrorist forces in any area where they might appear. In other words, neither the army commander nor the Chief of the General Staff issued any particular orders, but rather in this general directive it was determined that the strategic goal in the preparations in the course of January and February was to break-up these forces so that in March when the aggression was expected to begin the forces were ready to push back the forces, the NATO forces, coming from the Republic of Macedonia and the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, if you know, I've looked at all these orders up until the 16th of April and they all bear the heading "Joint Command" and they have no signature and they all carry the log numbers of the Pristina Corps, whereas after April 22nd, including the resubordination orders, all orders and decisions have the Pristina Corps heading and the log numbers of the Pristina Corps. Are these decisions the result of the coordination that you mentioned, the coordination that was done in 1998, so that pursuant to those orders MUP units which participate in these operations should join the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose -- well, General Radojko Stefanovic, who actually replaced me in the operations and training department, he probably continued to work in the same manner that we had done earlier. In other words, he would put "Joint Command" in the heading which would actually be an indication that there was coordination between the army and the MUP in keeping with the order issued by General Samardzic in 1998 and in early 1999 from -- the order from General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, regardless of the problems with resubordination, if there were any - and we can discuss this a little later - but beginning with the 20th of April and onwards, all decisions and orders had in their heading the words "the command of the Pristina Corps"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So this means that in this period the Pristina Corps issued orders that were then forwarded to police units that participated in those operations, and those units actually complied with those orders?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would appreciate it -- I'm not actually certain that that's how it was, and I was not really in a position to follow the work of General Stefanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see document D104 -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, do we see here "Joint Command" in the heading? Would you take a look? Can you confirm it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I see that you are jotting something. Would you please write down the number 455-56, that is the log-book and the number under which this order was filed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This order relates to the routing and destruction of the STS, Siptar terrorist forces, in the Malo Kosovo area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's dated 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at the last page of this order in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, can you see here that as the signature we see the words the Joint Command for KiM. Now, please keep this in mind, this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see D105, the Defence Exhibit D105.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, can we see here again that this -- this is a document produced by the Joint Command? We see that in the heading?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And we see the number, strictly confidential number 455-56/1. Now, can you tell us what this slash 1 refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that means that this is the same document with some version 1 or redaction 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. I see when I look at this that this is a similar document like the one we've seen before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is the subject of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject of this decision -- it says here it's an amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, forces in breaking up and destroying the STS in the area of Malo Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you describe -- could you please tell us what this amendment actually relates to, what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know in this particular case what this refers to. I know that General Lazarevic actually amended his decision -- or rather, point 4 of the decision because of the developments on the ground, because of certain circumstances that had changed. And he signed both that -- this amendment to the decision because the fourth item of this order, when we look at the entire document, can only be decided on by the unit commander, and no one but him can actually amend item 4. But since these amendments were done, General Lazarevic, although the previous order, 455-56, of 22nd of March, 1999, was not signed by General Lazarevic but rather in the signature we had the words "Joint Command," in this case he signs this order because there was an amendment to the agreement to what had been agreed at the MUP staff and with the MUP staff. And since these changes actually related to the military, he then forwarded this decision to his subordinate units so that they would know that he was the author of that amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But in the heading we still have the same number, and is this the log-book of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document D003-2555.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this order issued by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 25th of March ordering mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the 3rd Army comply with this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I think that this document has already been admitted into evidence as number 199. Perhaps I can get some assistance. Do you have number 199, D199?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel is correct. That document is Exhibit D199.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This was really helpful because I would have wanted to avoid admitting into evidence a document that has already been admitted. Could we now see document D004-3013.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm trying to go through this fast so I've already switched to the second page. I see that there's some initials here, DM/MC. I believe these initials are familiar. Could you tell us what the objective of this document was, why was it issued? I see under item 3 it says: "Continue to undertake combat operations with all army units to smash and destroy Siptar terrorists."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I drafted a large number of documents so I can only assume what this is about. So would you allow me a few moments just to read through it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm specifically referring you to item 3.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is an order to continue with combat operations with a purpose of routing and destroying Siptar terrorist forces because this is the time when the aggression had already begun. And in addition to its main task, which was to defend the borders and prevent the multi-national brigade to enter the territory and to defend the territorial borders, they also had this task to participate in the routing and destruction of Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is Exhibit D00344.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please just tell us briefly -- or rather, could you describe the difference between a command, an order, and a decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, a command can be -- or rather, an order can be a general type order which, as we've already seen, is not strictly speaking a command but certainly the objectives have to be implemented. Commands are also orders but of a special type. But a command would also include items. It would have to describe the enemy, the second item would be the neighbouring units, and the fourth item would be a decision which should also include the orders to subordinate units, the fourth, fifth, 16th or whatever the number of units that belong to it are. So the difference between an order and a command is that in a command an order begins with item 4, whereas in an order it begins with item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is there a difference whether an order is ordered -- is issued by a brigade or a lower unit or does it matter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it always bears the same name, order, but at the level of lower units it would be called a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we see 65 ter document 02812.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is an order of the 3rd Army command of the 29th of March, 1999, about regular combat reports, but in the introduction we can see that it's actually an elaboration of the order from the Supreme Command from the 27th of March, 1993 [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now to explain something. This report is called a regular combat report, is that a daily report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is from the lowest units going towards the top. So the lowest unit that compiles a report, does that report have to contain the noted problems in the combat actions, discipline matters, and so on, which are being reported to the immediately superior command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does have its format and the precise questions which are being reported on to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. What I'm interested in is the following. For example, we're in the middle of an action and my detachment has some problems. Would the report of the daily combat report of the -- being delivered to the command of the brigade, would that problem have to be referred to and the higher instance be informed about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these are matters that were discussed during coordination and there has been some deviation in terms of these matters and these matters have a significant influence on decisions of the commander of the military unit, such a report should then refer to these particular problems because they do affect the members of the army or the commander of the independent battalion or the brigade as the lowest command units that do provide a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So this problem then is reported from the brigade to the corps command, the corps command report to the army command about it, and then the army command would refer to the General Staff and inform them about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00345.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D180. It's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir. Can you please look at this exhibit and tell me if you have any information or did you have any information at that time. I am just going to tell you that this was the 7th of April, 1999, when the document was drafted. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Defence Exhibit D172, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were in the 3rd Army, were you familiar with this document, this indication or announcement of the directive?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Pristina, and in a conversation with the general he did point out that the directive was about to arrive because General Stojmirovic who was in Nis was the general that he was in regular contact with and I was in Kosovo, and so he let me know that the directive was on its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at exhibit -- 65 ter list 01448, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the army command. As far as I can see you did not participate in its drafting. Judging by the format, do you recognise ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would just like you to turn the page so that I can see exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page -- I don't see anyone other than general -- I don't see any signature -- anyone's signature other than General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that perhaps it wasn't me because it's about security, and if it's about some operative matter that has to do with security in any way and since he knows I was a security man before, he would usually give such documents to me. I would need to read a little bit of the document or perhaps you can point me to a specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, are you more familiar with this document now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this item, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the first page of the document and then you can see it. Yes, now we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You can see that during the restriction of movement period ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I have seen it before, but I do know about these patrols that were organised and the recognition signs that we set for during the night so that we could have mutual contacts and in view of the complex situation in order to avoid friendly fire between the MUP and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at paragraph 5 now. This is on page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Regardless of whether there were such cases or not, this was often repeated in orders to the commander to constantly keep reminding them of the duty of respecting international humanitarian law, to conduct themselves properly in terms of enemy soldiers, the civilian population, and so on. These matters were very often dealt with in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00346.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 65 ter list document 04049.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, were you aware of this document from the forward command post of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a little bit on the first page. Judging by this previous part and since I think my style of writing is a little bit different, I think that I did not draft this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat what he said, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is one of the superior officers at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is if we can -- you did not draft this document. I can see that the initials are DC/BV; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by a senior officer from the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And on the next page, item 4, did you ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an assignment allocating the focus of activities by the army and reminds the subordinate commanders to unify activities and actions in the area of all the forces where they happened to be. Joining together means coordination or coordinated action with neighbouring units, regardless of whether it was the MUP or other ministry organs, but this does not imply ordering. So this implies one form of coordinated action and joint action, but it does not imply orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please, Your Honours. And I would like to first ask -- I don't know now what the calculation of the time is. Should I continue, or should we make a break at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're perfectly on time. This is our first break. That document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be Exhibit D00347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, as for the speed, I think that we have established a good rhythm, so we can continue without being warned by the ladies and gentlemen from the interpreting booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at 65 ter list Exhibit 04054.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we can see here an order for the defence of the Pristina Corps command of the 6th of April, 1998. This is the command for defence of the Pristina Corps. And then we can see that this has been classified as a state secret, and then it says Grom, Thunder, 4. The date is the 6th of April, 1998, on the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be a difficulty with that, is there not, Mr. Djurdjic? The original appears to be 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would stipulate that the English translation should be 1999 instead of 1998. I think this came up in Milutinovic and we agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The content would suggest it's 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I am reading the original document in the Serbian so I didn't really pay attention to the translation of the date, but I think that it is clear that it's just a typo because the original document has the date of 1999 and this is also indicated by the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain Grom 4, Thunder 4, what that means.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to explain right away that there has been a mistake here. Instead of "Thunder" as it says in the directive of the General Staff, there is a mistake at the army command level down to the Pristina Corps, where we have Thunder 4. In the period of preparation for the previous trial of Mr. Milutinovic and others, General Stojmirovic, who was the Chief of Staff in the Nis 3rd Army command, who was leading the drafting of the command at the 3rd Army command level, when the senior officer received the command from the General Staff because the previous one was Thunder 3, he thought that Grom 3 -- 4 had been skipped, so then he added it. But actually the command Thunder 4 at the army and the corps level is a product of the command for Thunder from General Ojdanic which does not have any numerical marking. This is the essence. The only mistake is that this person added the number 4 because he believed that somebody in the General Staff missed the number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe this is an administrative error, but what I would like you to do is tell us a bit about the content actually.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a command for defence against the aggression. The aggression was already ongoing. The Siptar terrorist forces broke into the territory of Kosovo from Albania and the army took up positions in defence areas along the border from the border with Montenegro all the way to the Bulgarian border in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army command, practically the entire border with Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please explain whether, as a result of this command, decisions and commands that were issued on the 6th, 9th, 14th, 15th, and 16th April, 1999 - and I'm referring to actions Zatric Selo, Jezerce Selo, Bajgora, Bare, Cicavica, Orlane, Las, Drenica, Zegovac -- do you know of this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did know about this. There was no doubt anymore that an all-out attack was impending on the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army. And in keeping with our combat rules, the army, pursuant to the task that was issued to it, proceeded to rout and break up terrorist forces in the areas -- in their areas in the -- in direct combat. And this was as part of the preparations for defence against the overall aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So to put this in lay terms, the purpose was to neutralise the terrorist Albanian forces before the aggression actually begins, the land aggression, because they knew that they would then strike us from the back?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a task that could not be done in one go. It was a task that was ongoing, and it would be ongoing during the combat operations. The first echelon, which means the brigades in the forward positions, the 125th, 549th, and 156th Infantry Brigade which were towards Macedonia, while they would put up defence operations, the others, the 15th Armoured Brigade, the 252nd Tactical Group, the 211th Armoured Brigade in the area of Podujevo municipality, they all had the task to build up positions and organise firing systems. And part of their forces were to fight the terrorists and sabotage groups because those groups were attacking the artillery and the rear and taking up the important positions on -- on crossroads and bridges and so on. So the general task of the army was defence and then the -- another task that was comprised in that was the fighting against terrorist and sabotage groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, in view of the position that you occupied, could you tell us whether any of these commands or orders, especially the ones that were issued between the 26th -- or rather, the 24th of March, when the war began, up until the end of the war, and specifically up until April 15th, were any of these directed against the civilian population, the Albanian civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, in 1998 and 1999 there was something in the commands that was perhaps never, up until then, regulated by any army, such as the deployment of units whose task was to pull out the civilian population from the threat -- from the areas where fighting was fierce. So they -- these units were tasked with the task of pulling out and protecting -- pulling out, withdrawing the civilian population from the areas where the fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that villages that were encircled -- do you know of instances where villages that were encircled were bombed and civilians attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure I understood your question. Do you mean that they were bombed by us, by our side?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know that there was any such plan, that they would bomb them and then soldiers would come into the villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such plans and such operations I don't know of, which does not mean that there weren't some civilian casualties, as, for instance, in Lipljani, where a group of civilians were killed -- and this was even taken to court but no one was convicted because there was insufficient evidence that there was intent to kill these individuals. I personally do not know of any cases, of a single case, that anything like this was done in a planned way and that there were deliberate civilian casualties by mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you said now that you didn't know of this, that you didn't know that there was any of this envisaged in any of these orders or commands, but do you know of any such instances in fact that villages were encircled and civilians expelled from there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at any level of command. This was never -- no such orders were ever issued, nor was anything like that ever done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00348.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Defence Exhibit D183.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we see here a directive from the Supreme Command Staff dated 9th April, 1999. I would now like to tie this in with that command and directive from January. Now, could you tell us whether there were any changes relayed between these two, were there any changes in the tasks for the units of the 3rd Army Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a big difference between that directive and this one. The January directive provided for the engagement of forces of the Pristina Corps, or rather, the 3rd Army in the routing of sabotage and terrorist groups and preparations for the defence against the multi-national brigade of NATO whose advance was expected. This was a directive whereby the General Staff was developing a plan of opposition to the NATO forces in the event that they would attack the country or enter the country. Now, this directive here is a direct order for taking up positions, defence positions, and raising the level of combat-readiness of units in order for them to be ready to fight the units that would make incursions from the territory of Albania. So this is a defence plan, whereas the other one related to a plan against the NATO advances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to take a look at another document, D187.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is an order from the Supreme Command Staff of 15 April 1999, ordering information to be provided to them. I can -- I see that this was also sent to the 3rd Army. Now, was -- was there any information coming in pursuant to this order as far as the 3rd Army was concerned and the staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything in item 1. There are no changes whatsoever. This is the standard format. There are no amendments. The second item, to check the veracity of information, that is something that was implied. There was nothing novel in this. I don't see any major differences in the third item either. In essence, all of this was something that was already in force; but when the Chief of the General Staff issued his directive, he stressed this problem in view of the fact that a high-intensity armed conflict was anticipated. And I think that this was the only reason why the Chief of the General Staff actually issued this directive because pursuant to those reports he would make his decisions. So that is the purpose of this. In any other sense there are no changes or differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me just put you a lay question. Is this -- does this relate to written reports, combat reports that would be sent to their units that would then be referred to higher commands, or are these reports that are sent via the signals or communications system?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This relates to reports that would be sent through combat reports and operations departments, because we see here that it is -- that stress is put on the operations officer who is at the duty centre who prepares these combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you are in the command of the 3rd Army. Up until this date and after this date as well, there have been certain weaknesses and certain irregularities in conducting combat operations. Now, would you or did you refer such information, the information that you received from units, would you have to refer this to the higher -- to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This had to be done and on the basis of the corps units and independent units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So lower-level units would send this to the corps command, and then the corps command would send it to their higher-ups; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Defence Exhibit D004-3017.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, would you please read this document to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is report number 23 from the Supreme Command Staff, the intelligence administration.
